## Goals

- Confirm R, RStudio, and Quarto are installed and working
- Get comfortable with the RStudio panes and project workflow
- Write and run your first few lines of R

## Installation check

Run this chunk. If it errors, come to office hours or post on Canvas
for install help — don't struggle with this alone before Week 2.

```{r}
#| label: setup
r_version <- R.version.string
r_version
library(tidyverse)
```

## File types you'll see in this course

| Extension | What it is |
|---|---|
| `.R` | Plain R script |
| `.qmd` | Quarto document (code + prose, like this file) |
| `.Rproj` | RStudio project file — keeps file paths relative |
| `.csv` / `.xlsx` | Tabular data |
| `.html` / `.pdf` | Rendered output from a `.qmd` |

## Your first R

```{r}
# Assignment
wing_length <- c(23.1, 25.4, 22.8, 26.0, 24.3)

# Basic functions
mean(wing_length)
sd(wing_length)
length(wing_length)
```

```{r}
# Indexing
wing_length[1]
wing_length[wing_length > 24]
```

## Your first plot

A small reward for getting everything installed:

```{r}
#| label: fig-first-plot
#| fig-cap: "A first look at some simulated wing lengths"
tibble(wing_length) |>
  ggplot(aes(wing_length)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Exercises

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise 1
Create a vector `body_mass` with 5 values of your choosing (grams).
Compute its mean, standard deviation, and range using built-in
functions (don't hardcode the answers).
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise 2
In a sentence or two: why might a biologist care about *designing*
an experiment carefully, rather than just collecting data and running
a statistical test afterward? There's no single right answer — this
is meant to get you thinking ahead of Week 5.
:::

## Wrap-up

Keep this file — the exercises here feed directly into this week's
